doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

chapter: Black Radio and the new waves
title: Live band versus DJ-mixed jazz and hip-hop
summary: Asked about earlier jazz-rap, he says his Experiment band plays jazz, hip-hop and R&B itself, unlike a DJ mixing jazz in.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I would say it’s a precursor to the two wave. You’ve got Digable Planets. You had “Guru,” it’s a jazz thing, that was early 90s.
So a lot of those things were the D.J. mixing the jazz in.

Yeah. Because the thing I like about my band, especially the experiment band, which is different from most, because a lot of people, I’ve had smart alecks after me, “that’s been done before, what are you doin’ different?” Like well we’re one band. Like we’re one band playing hip-hop, playing jazz, and playing R&B to a very high level. To the point where the jazz cats are like, “y’all the best jazz group we’ve ever heard.” And then hip- hop, the Roots, Amir is like, “y’all play hip-hop the best.” You know what I mean? One band getting that kind of credit and playing all those things is different than a D.J. playing the jazz part and mixing in the saxophone. You know. Or scratching. You know. You know. And so that’s the difference, and it’s the live band aspect and people playing all these different genres themselves and not needing a D.J., “okay, you’re the hip-hop part.” You know. Now we’re mixing jazz and hip-hop. That’s been done before. You know what I mean?
